lines.text: Rich cloth towns and master painters, a young kingdom fought over in two world wars, and now the capital of Europe. This is the story of Belgium.
It begins in Bruges, a town of canals that grew from the ninth century into the richest trading city of northern Europe.
In the fifteenth century, Jan van Eyck perfected painting in oils, catching jewels, fur and light in astonishing detail.
In Brussels, the town hall began to rise over the Grand-Place, a square that came to be ringed by the houses of the guilds.
In 1432, the van Eyck brothers finished the Ghent Altarpiece, a landmark of oil painting that would be stolen and hidden many times.
A century later, Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted crowded villages and snowy hunters, the everyday life of the Low Countries.
In Antwerp, Peter Paul Rubens ran a busy workshop, filling churches and palaces with lively Baroque paintings, and served as a diplomat besides.
In June 1815, at Waterloo, just south of Brussels, Wellington and the Prussians defeated Napoleon for the last time.
Fifteen years later, in 1830, the south rose against Dutch rule in a revolution that split it from the Netherlands.
So a new country was born: Belgium, a kingdom of Dutch, French and German speakers.
Its second king, Leopold the second, would build a vast fortune by ruling a colony in Africa as his own property.
In his Congo Free State, forced labour for rubber and ivory killed vast numbers of people, until outrage abroad made Belgium take it over in 1908.
Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian priest and physicist, would propose that the universe began from a tiny dense state, the idea behind the Big Bang.
Rene Magritte would paint a pipe that is not a pipe, and men in bowler hats, the gentle puzzles of Belgian surrealism.
And Herge would create Tintin, making Brussels a capital of comics.
In 1912, a chocolate maker in Brussels invented the filled praline, and Belgian chocolate found its fame.
Two years later, Germany invaded neutral Belgium, and Britain entered the First World War.
Around Ypres that autumn, the armies dug in, and the trenches of the Western Front took shape.
In 1917, at Passchendaele, a British-led offensive sank into rain and mud, gaining little ground at a terrible cost.
In 1929, Tintin set off on his first adventure, with his dog Snowy. He would be read in over seventy languages.
War came again. In the winter of 1944, Germany's last great offensive in the west burst through the Ardennes forest, and was beaten back.
Eddy Merckx, born in 1945, would win the Tour de France five times and be called by many the greatest cyclist of all.
In 1949, Belgium helped found NATO, the alliance that would later make Brussels its home.
In 1958, the new European Commission set up in Brussels to run the young European Community.
That same year, the Atomium rose over the city, nine steel spheres meant to stand for just a few months.
It was the symbol of Expo 58, the first great world's fair after the war, where America and the Soviet Union built rival pavilions.
And so Brussels became the home of Europe's main institutions, the closest thing the continent has to a capital.
Bart De Wever, a Flemish nationalist born in 1970, would become prime minister in 2025, in a country whose regions had won ever more self-rule.
In March 2016, suicide bombers struck Brussels airport and a metro station, killing thirty-two people.
From the cloth halls of Bruges to the heart of Europe, Belgium keeps finding its place between larger neighbours.
